M2 · Power-factor correction, three-phase and equivalent-circuit tests (Ch2)

Why this matters in the exam: Question 1 (20 marks) is “AC and DC Power Circuit Analysis” in both past papers, and this topic fills most of it. Jun23 Q1a (battery model, 5 marks) and Q1b (star vs delta, 6 marks) make 11 of the 20 marks. Jun24 Q1d (power-factor correction, 8 marks) is the biggest single part of that year’s Q1. PFC comes back in Q4: Jun23 Q4b (7 marks, plant PFC with a synchronous motor) and Jun23 Q4c(i) (short answer, “explain power-factor correction”). Expect 15–25 of your 80 marks to use this pack’s methods.

Notation follows the course and your Test Reference. Subscript 1 = phase quantity (), subscript L = line quantity. is the angle of the current relative to the voltage: lagging means . All values are rms.

1. The core ideas

1.1 The power triangle and its signs

Element P Q Current vs voltage
Resistor absorbs, 0 in phase
Inductor (motor, ballast) 0 absorbs, lags
Capacitor 0 generates, leads
  • When to use: every AC power question.
  • Trap: . The square root does not give the sign. Inductive means , capacitive means .
  • For loads in parallel, add the P values and add the Q values. Never add S values.

1.2 Power-factor correction (PFC)

A capacitor goes in parallel with the load (across the supply). It generates reactive power locally, so the supply carries less.

Quantity Changes with C?
Supply real power No. Capacitors absorb no real power.
Load’s own P, Q, current, pf No. The load still sees the same voltage.
Supply Q, S, current Yes. They fall until unity pf, then rise again.
Supply pf Rises to 1 at , then becomes leading.

Key formulas:

  • When to use: “find the capacitance to raise the pf to …”, “what pf results from C = …”.
  • Trap: is the voltage across the capacitor. In three-phase this is the phase voltage of the bank, and it depends on star or delta (section 1.4).
  • Trap: a leading target pf gives . So one pf value has two capacitor solutions: under-corrected (lagging) and over-corrected (leading).

Slide C up from zero: P stays fixed while Q, S and the supply current fall to a minimum at unity pf, then rise again as the pf turns leading.

1.3 Three-phase: star vs delta

Star (Y) Delta ()
Voltage
Current
Power (both) same

  • is always the angle between phase voltage and phase current. The three-phase pf equals the pf of one phase.
  • Assume star unless told otherwise. “415 V, 4.8 A, 2.2 kW” means line voltage, line current, total (output) power (Practice Q2.23e–f).
  • Same impedances, same supply, star changed to delta: rises by , rises by , rises by 3, and P, Q, S all rise by 3. The pf does not change (lecture 2.8.4).
  • Trap: using in the power formula with phase quantities, or 3 with line quantities.

1.4 Capacitor banks: why star or delta matters

Each of the three capacitors supplies one third of . Its voltage depends on the connection.

  • A delta bank needs one third of the capacitance. But each capacitor must be rated for the full line voltage.
  • A star bank needs 3 times the capacitance, rated for .
  • The line current into the bank is the same in both cases (same , same ).
  • Trap: a bank sized for delta and then wired in star supplies only one third of the vars.

1.5 DC source (battery) model

The model is an ideal source in series with an internal resistance (lecture 1.1.3, 2.1.7).

  • When to use: “open-circuit voltage measured … voltage falls to … when drawing …”.
  • Trap: the loss in is , not with the terminal voltage. Maximum power happens at only 50% efficiency, so we avoid operating there (Practice Q2.8).

Worked example 2: your Prac 1 PFC test (Table 5 data)

Given: from your Prac 1 report, the series-RL load (load 5) draws about W and VAr at V, 50 Hz. These are the averages of the “LOAD” columns in Table 5. The capacitors tested were 9, 12, 18, 36 and 54 µF. Find: (a) C for 0.9 lag, (b) C for unity pf, (c) check the measured supply Q values.

(a) does not change. VAr.

This matches your B.3 answer (16.4 µF, from P = 24.5 W and Q = 30.5 VAr at 60 V). The 18 µF test point gave a measured pf of 0.902, just above 0.9, as expected.

(b) 27.0 µF. Your report estimates about 28.6 µF for unity pf. The theory line crosses zero at 27.0 µF, so re-check how you read that value off your graph.

(c) Use the rule from the prac sheet: supply Q ≈ load Q + capacitor Q.

C (µF) Load Q Capacitor Q (meas.) Sum Table 5 supply Q Theory
9 30.7 −11.0 19.7 20.7 20.5
12 31.2 −14.9 16.3 17.7 17.3
18 30.7 −22.1 8.6 11.9 10.1
36 31.0 −45.3 −14.3 +16.6 −10.7
54 31.0 −67.7 −36.7 −36.4 −31.3

At 36 µF the supply Q must be negative (over-corrected, leading). The +16.6 is a LabVIEW sign error and should be marked −16.6*. So the “0.837” pf at 36 µF is leading, not lagging. The measured capacitor vars are about 7% larger than . The real capacitors behave like about 1.07 × their nominal value (for example, 22.1 VAr at 18 µF implies 19.3 µF). That is why the measured points at high C sit below the theory line.

The right-hand plot shows the “two solutions” effect: pf = 0.9 happens at 16.4 µF (lagging) and at 37.5 µF (leading).

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Wrong sign of . A capacitor generates vars, so . In Jun24 Q1d(ii) the answer is VAr, not +21.25. Then use in .
  • Using the wrong . Jun24 Q1d(iii) gives a new VAr. Using −21.25 VAr from part (ii) gives 4.26 µF, which is wrong. The answer is 6.017 µF.
  • Forgetting 60 Hz. Jun24 Q1d(iii) and Practice Q2.20 use 60 Hz ( rad/s). Read the frequency every time.
  • Changing P during PFC. The supply P is the same before and after. Only Q, S, I and the pf change.
  • Using the line voltage for a star bank. Each star capacitor sees . Using undersizes the bank by a factor of 3.
  • Mixing up and 3. Use with phase values and with line values. In delta, , so Jun23 Q1b(ii) has A but A.
  • Not stating lead or lag. A pf without “lag” or “lead” loses the mark. Over-correction gives a leading pf, as at 36 µF in your prac.
  • Using the series formula for a parallel model (or the reverse). needs the current through R. In a parallel model only works.

Solution

Hint: the synchronous motor generates its spare vars: .

  1. 235.3 kW and +158.1 kVAr.

  2. 222.2 kW. Its 250 kVA rating limits , so the most reactive power it can supply is 114.6 kVAr (generated, so kVAr). Unrounded this is 114.5 kVAr.

  3. kW and kVAr, so the best plant pf is 0.9955 lag.

N4. [8 marks] A workshop on a 415 V, 50 Hz three-phase supply has an induction motor delivering 22 kW of mechanical output at 90% efficiency and 0.82 pf lag, and a 10 kW balanced resistive heater.

  1. Find the total P, Q and pf of the workshop, and the line current. [3]
  2. Find the reactive power a capacitor bank must supply to raise the pf to 0.98 lag. [2]
  3. Find the capacitance per phase if the bank is connected in delta, and if it is connected in star. Which needs the higher voltage rating? [2]
  4. The delta-sized capacitors are wired in star by mistake. What pf results? [1]
Solution
  1. Motor input: kW and kVAr. The heater adds 10 kW and 0 kVAr.

  1. kVAr, so −10.07 kVAr (−3.356 kVAr per capacitor).

  2. Delta: 62.0 µF, rated 415 V. Star: 186.1 µF, rated 240 V. The delta bank needs the higher voltage rating. The new line current is A.

  3. In star each 62.0 µF capacitor sees only 239.6 V, so the bank supplies kVAr. Then kVAr and pf 0.929 lag.

N5. [7 marks] (Uses your Prac 1 data.) The series-RL prac load absorbs 25.0 W and +31.0 VAr from a 60.5 V, 50 Hz supply.

  1. Find the supply current and pf without correction. [1]
  2. Find the two values of parallel capacitance that give a supply pf of 0.9. State whether each gives a leading or lagging pf. [3]
  3. Find the supply current for both values in (b), and the minimum possible supply current. [1]
  4. In Table 5 the 36 µF row shows supply Q = +16.6 VAr with load Q = 31.0 VAr and capacitor Q = −45.3 VAr. Explain why the sign must be wrong, and state whether the 0.837 pf is leading or lagging. [2]
Solution

  1. VA, 0.658 A (Table 5 measured ≈ 0.658 A), and pf 0.628 lag.

  2. , so VAr.

  • Lagging: gives VAr and 16.4 µF (lag).
  • Leading: gives VAr and 37.5 µF (lead).

  1. Both give VA, so 0.459 A in both cases. The minimum current is at unity pf: 0.413 A.

  2. Reactive power is conserved: VAr. That is negative, so the supply value must be −16.6 VAr. The circuit is over-corrected and the 0.837 pf is leading.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

POWER TRIANGLE   S = V I* = P + jQ = S∠-φ   P = S cosφ   Q = S sin(-φ)   pf = P/S
  φ = current angle wrt voltage: lag φ<0, Q>0 (L) | lead φ>0, Q<0 (C). Sign of Q from physics, not √.
  Parallel loads: add P's, add Q's (never S's).

PFC (C in parallel; P never changes)
  1 P, Q_old   2 Q_S = +P tan(acos pf) lag / -P tan(...) lead / 0 unity
  3 Q_C = Q_S - Q_old (<0)   4 C = |Q_C|/(ω V²), V across C, check 50 vs 60 Hz
  5 S_new = P/pf, I_new = S_new/V.  Reverse: Q_C = -ωCV², Q_S = Q_old + Q_C
  One pf -> two C values (under/over-corrected). Over-correction -> leading, I rises.

3-PHASE (assume star; ratings = line V, line I, total P)
  Star: VL = √3 V1, IL = I1      Delta: VL = V1, IL = √3 I1
  S = 3V1I1 = √3 VL IL;  P = √3 VL IL cosφ;  pf(3ph) = pf(1 phase)
  Same Z: star -> delta on same supply: I1, V1 ×√3; IL, P, Q, S ×3; pf same
  Cap bank, |Q_C|/3 each:  C_Y = |Q_C|/(ω VL²)  [rated VL/√3]
                           C_Δ = |Q_C|/(3 ω VL²) [rated VL]     C_Y = 3 C_Δ

BATTERY   V = E - I Rs;  E = Voc;  Rs = (Voc - V)/I = Voc/Isc
          loss = I² Rs;  Pmax = E²/(4Rs) at RL = Rs (η = 50%)

V,I,P TESTS   S = VI, Q = +√(S²-P²)
  series: R = P/I², X = Q/I²     parallel: R = V²/P, X = V²/Q
  L = X/ω, C = 1/(ω|X|). 3ph: per phase first (V1 = VL/√3, P1 = P/3).
